note: Bz is the leading indicator and Kp is the lagging one. A southward interplanetary field is what actually opens the door, and DSCOVR sits far enough upstream to give a quarter-hour to an hour of warning - which is the difference between a readout that says 'this quarter-day was quiet' and one that says 'go now'.
Speed and density from the same spacecraft. Bz southward with a fast wind behind it is the combination worth driving for.
The G1-G5 watches and warnings, so a storm surfaces on its own rather than waiting for somebody to open the panel and check.

Three attempts at PAD-US, three 400s, and the last said Invalid URL for the service root rather than the query - so the path shape is wrong, not the parameters. This prints each service beside its type instead of assuming FeatureServer a fourth time.

The closer route to BLM polygons: the surface-management service the public lands layer already uses. If its sublayer answers a bbox query with geometry, hatching becomes a styling decision and PAD-US stops mattering.

What the MVUM service says it holds. The raster we draw is layers=show:1,2, but a click has to name a sublayer to identify against, and the field a road's class lives in is whatever this says it is. Printing the sublayer list and their fields is the whole of what is needed to design the panel.

Three real roads out of Shawnee National Forest with every field, so the panel is written against the attributes the service actually returns rather than the ones the MVUM legend implies. Seasonal dates and permitted vehicle classes are the two the reader wants and the two most likely to be named something unguessable.
The same question of the BLM route service. It draws four sublayers and the panel needs to know which one a given line came from before it can say anything about it.
Three real BLM routes in central Utah with every field. GTLF publishes route designations - open, limited, closed, and to which vehicle types - and this is what says under which names.

The field list for Motor Vehicle Use Map: Roads, with each field's type. This is the authoritative answer to what a road's class, its seasonal dates and its permitted vehicle types are actually called - the first pass asked for the attributes and got back only the word 'attributes', which was a bad regex rather than a quiet service.

The same for the first BLM route sublayer. GTLF names its designation in the sublayer itself - 'Roads Managed for Public Motorized Use' and seven others - so the per-feature fields may add route number, surface and season on top of that rather than repeating it.

The question the whole change turns on. M-22 through Leland: if a Michigan state route arrives with a shape value it gets Michigan's own diamond, and sending the unknowns to a circle is safe. If it arrives as `default` like the county road two miles away did, then the two are indistinguishable and a circle default would strip the M off every state route in the state.
M-72 near Traverse City, because one road is not a rule and a single sample that happened to be tagged well would be the worst possible evidence.
A Leelanau county road again, at a second point, to confirm the county side of the pair really is `default` rather than that one road being untagged.
And Tennessee, whose SR 61 started all of this - so the fallback change can be checked against a state whose routes are known to arrive with a shape.
